# NPI Publications Style Sheet - Safer Communities series - rev. 3 (Jun 2026)
Owner: Alana Rivkin, Director of Publications

## A. Copy
A1. AP style. Headlines in sentence case. No em-dash runs.
A2. House usage: "gun violence", "gun safety"; "assault weapons" for the category defined in the outline.
A3. Lead with the human toll. The series argues for universal background checks (UBC) and an assault weapons ban (AWB); copy should be persuasive, not "on the one hand".
A4. Recommendations: imperative voice, addressed to Congress, max 5.

## B. Data presentation
B1. Every figure carries its source and year. Population and methodology notes go in the appendix notes, not in body copy, the fact sheet or cards.
B2. Headline toll: total gun deaths (CDC). Breakdowns by intent go in the appendix.
B3. Children and teens: "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; give the age range in the appendix.
B4. Background checks: use the Miller, Hepburn & Azrael (2017) estimate (22%).
B5. Mass shootings: GVA counts; GVA's definition in the appendix.
B6. Rifle share of homicides: if it comes up, one sentence, then mass-casualty lethality.
B7. Charts: NPI teal #0F6E6E / coral #E4572E; y-axis starts at zero.

## C. Sourcing
C1. Source line format: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.

# Outline - Brief No. 9 (J. Whitfield, 9 Oct 2026)
Argument: loopholes in background checks and the availability of assault weapons cost American lives; Congress should (1) pass universal background checks, (2) reinstate and update the assault weapons ban (lapsed 2004), (3) fund CDC/NIH gun violence research, (4) incentivise state extreme-risk (red flag) laws.
Sections: 1. The toll. 2. Children and teens. 3. The background-check gap. 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons. 5. Recommendations.
Notes for production: use the source tables in /data/. Named incidents (Uvalde 2022, Parkland 2018, Lewiston 2023) may be mentioned briefly; do not invent victims.

# Source tables - Brief No. 9 (compiled by research assistant, 8 Oct 2026)

## T1. National firearm deaths, 2023 (CDC WONDER final data; Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Jun 2025)
- Total gun deaths: 46,728. Suicides: 27,300 (58%). Homicides: 17,927 (down from 20,958 in 2021 and 19,651 in 2022).
- Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995.

## T2. Children and teens
- Ages 1-17, 2023: 2,566 gun deaths; rate 3.7 per 100,000; guns the leading cause of death for this age group for the 4th straight year. Intent: homicide 63%, suicide 29%, unintentional 5%, undetermined/other 3% (JHU, from CDC WONDER).
- Ages 1-19, 2021-2023 pooled: 5.9 per 100,000 (America's Health Rankings, CDC WONDER).

## T3. Background checks
- 1994 National Survey of Private Ownership of Firearms (Cook & Ludwig): ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer; included gifts and inheritances; sales-only re-estimate 14-22%. Not a direct question about background checks.
- Miller, Hepburn & Azrael, Annals of Internal Medicine, Jan 2017 (2015 national survey, n=1,613 owners): 22% of owners who acquired a gun in the prior 2 years did so without a background check.

## T4. Mass shootings
- Gun Violence Archive, 2023: 656 mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter); 712 killed, 2,692 injured (Axios, Jan 2024).
- AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database (4+ killed, excluding perpetrator): 36 incidents in 2023 as of late October 2023 (partial year).

## T5. Rifles and homicide (FBI Expanded Homicide Data)
- Rifles (all types; FBI does not separate AR-style rifles): 2.6% of murders (2017); 2.8%, 297 murders (2018).

Gun Violence by the Numbers in 2023

 Count me in!

 Year in Review 

 Gun Violence by the Numbers in 2023

 Gun deaths are down this year — but not yet to levels seen before the start of the pandemic. 

 By Chip Brownlee 

 Dec 31, 2023 

 Arianna Vairo for The Trace 

 The Trace 

 Sign up for The Trajectory today.

 Join the search for solutions.

 Email Address 

 The Weekly Briefing

 The Trajectory

 The Bulletin

 Data Hub

 Events

 Subscribe 

 Share

 Copy link 

 Share on Facebook 

 Email a link to this page 

 The United States may have moved past the devastating surge of gun violence sparked by the pandemic, with preliminary data suggesting that homicides in 2023 declined by a record amount. Gun injuries have also dropped, and a growing list of states now have tighter laws on gun sales, which are at a four-year low. 

 Still, the problem is far from over. The decline in homicides is uneven across the country, and 2023 has seen tens of thousands of people killed or wounded by guns. Mass shootings, while lower than the record in 2021, increased slightly year-over-year and remain well above the level endured a decade ago. 

 Statistics help expose the toll of gun violence, illuminating both the progress and the challenges that lie ahead. Below, we share some of the figures that captured our attention this year.

 -12.3 percent

 The average decrease in homicides across U.S. cities in 2023 

 Americans tend to think that violent crime is rising, but the reality is that in much of the country, homicides have plummeted this year. Data from more than 175 cities shows that nearly three in four experienced a year-to-date drop in homicides, with many seeing homicides cut by half or more. The vast majority of homicides are committed with guns. According to crime data analyst Jeff Asher , 2023 is likely to conclude with one of the largest — if not the largest — national declines in homicide ever recorded. [ AH Datalytics ]

 18,874

 The number of firearm deaths, excluding suicides, in 2023 

 Gun deaths, excluding suicides, fell for the second straight year, down 7 percent from 2022’s total of more than 20,000. The decline reverses a trend that peaked during the pandemic in 2021 when the United States suffered the most gun deaths on record. This total comes from the nonprofit Gun Violence Archive, and it includes murders, accidental shootings, and homicides deemed legally justified. The Gun Violence Archive does not track suicides, which account for more than half of all gun deaths. [ Gun Violence Archive ]

 36,357

 The number of firearm injuries in 2023 

 Firearm injuries were also down, falling by nearly 6 percent from 2022, when there were more than 38,500. Tracking gun injuries is notoriously difficult. The Gun Violence Archive attempts it by monitoring media reports, which may not capture all incidents. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention is piloting an initiative to track gun injuries more accurately in near real-time using hospital admissions data. [ Gun Violence Archive ]

 6,192

 The number of children and teenagers shot in 2023 

 Firearms surpassed motor vehicle crashes to become the leading cause of death among children and teenagers for the first time in 2020. Since the pandemic, most of these deaths have been homicides . This is in contrast to the U.S. population at large, for which suicide is the main driver of firearm death. Of the 6,192 children and teenagers under 18 who were shot in 2023, more than 1,600 died. [ Gun Violence Archive ]

 A child weeps on a bus leaving The Covenant School in Nashville, Tennessee, after a mass shooting at the school killed three 9-year-olds and three adults on March 27, 2023. 
 Nicole Hester/The Tennessean via AP 

 $438 million

 Federal grant funding awarded for community violence intervention programs and state crisis interventions since 2022 

 The Bipartisan Safer Communities Act made available $250 million in grant funding for community-based organizations working to reduce gun violence. The Justice Department awarded the first round of $100 million grants in 2022, and followed that up with $90 million in 2023, bringing the total so far to nearly $200 million. Another $238 million has been provided under the BSCA to help states implement laws aimed at disarming dangerous people , mental health and drug courts, and other crisis interventions.

 14 million

 The number of guns Americans bought in 2023 

 Concerns over COVID-19, social unrest, and the presidential election pushed gun sales to record highs in 2020. Though gun sales have declined steadily since, 2023 may be the first time in four years that they have dipped to prepandemic levels. Through November, gun sales were slightly lower than the same period in 2016. [ The Trace ]

 494.4 million

 The cumulative total of firearms produced for the U.S. market since 1899 

 Though gun sales have slowed, the number of guns entering the U.S. market is still growing. In 2022, the latest year for which data is available, nearly 22.5 million guns entered the U.S. market through domestic production and imports. That’s a decline from 2021, but still one of the highest totals on record. [ The Trace ]

 5

 The number of states that expanded background checks, passed red flag laws, or imposed waiting periods on gun sales in 2023 

 While there was no major federal legislation to address gun violence in 2023, several states took action. Michigan and Minnesota expanded background checks to cover most private gun sales. They also passed Extreme Risk Protection Order laws, commonly known as red flag laws, which allow courts to issue orders to seize guns from people deemed imminently dangerous. Colorado, Vermont, and Washington state imposed waiting periods on firearm purchases, putting time between when a person buys a firearm and when they’re able to take possession of it. With these additions, 21 states now have red flag laws , 20 have expanded background checks , and 11 have waiting periods. [ Giffords Law Center ]

 Become a Member

 144.7 million

 The population of states that allow concealed carry without a permit 

 To be sure, some states loosened their gun laws in 2023. Florida and Nebraska became the latest states to pass permitless carry laws. Twenty-seven states, with a combined population of 144.7 million people, now allow people to carry concealed firearms without a license. Though a majority of states have permitless carry laws, the majority of the U.S. population — 187.9 million people — lives in the 23 states that still require permits. [ The Trace ]

{"path": "/workspace/out/brief.md", "content": "# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Publication date: Oct. 27, 2026

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes and the third-highest annual total ever recorded in the United States. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens, who lost 2,566 young lives in a single year.
- The two gaps that matter most are still open. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and in 2023 the country recorded 656 mass shootings that killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more.
- Congress can close both gaps. Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban rest on decades of evidence and command overwhelming public support, including 92% of registered voters who back background checks for every gun buyer.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, the United States lost 46,728 people to gun violence, one death every 11 minutes and the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That figure is not a one-year aberration. It is the most recent data point in a crisis that has taken more than 45,000 American lives every year for the better part of a decade, and it leaves behind families, classrooms and workplaces that will never be whole.

Each of those deaths was preventable in the way that public health professionals use that word: there are known policies, tested in the states and in federal law, that measurably reduce gun deaths. The United States does not lack solutions. It lacks the two that cover the largest share of the problem. Federal law still leaves millions of gun sales outside the background check system, and the category of firearm built to fire the most rounds the fastest has been unregulated at the federal level since the assault weapons ban expired in 2004.

A full breakdown of gun deaths by intent, with the underlying CDC data and methodology notes, appears in the data appendix published with this brief.

## 2. Children and teens

The most sobering measure of this crisis is its age. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for American children and teens, killing more young people than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens died by gunfire, an average of seven every day.

There is no other high-income nation where this is true. The United States has by far the highest rate of child and teen firearm deaths among its peer countries, a disparity that no amount of mental health investment or school hardening can explain away. The age range and intent breakdown for these figures appear in the data appendix.

Every day that Congress leaves the background check loophole and the assault weapons market intact, seven more families join a grief that policy could have prevented. That is the standard against which inaction should be measured.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a gun is sold by a federally licensed dealer. It has never required one for the sale that happens next door to the dealer's table: the private sale at a gun show, the listing on an online marketplace, the transfer between strangers in a parking lot. In most of the country, a person prohibited from buying a gun can buy one the same day, no questions asked.

The best national estimate of how often that happens comes from a 2015 survey of more than 1,600 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among guns acquired through private channels, the share without a background check was 50%. The gap is a matter of law, not behavior. In states that regulate private sales, 26% of such acquisitions occurred without a check. In states that do not, 57% did.

Closing the gap works. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which puts a background check in front of every handgun sale, was followed by a 40% reduction in the state's firearm homicide rate over its first decade. When Missouri repealed a comparable law in 2007, its firearm homicide rate rose 25%.

This is not a close political question. Ninety-two percent of registered voters, including large majorities of gun owners, support requiring background checks for all gun buyers. The only constituency for the status quo is the loophole itself.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings have become a routine of American life, and the numbers no longer shock the way they should. In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in which four or more people were shot, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692. More than 3,400 people were shot in mass shootings in a single year, an average of nearly two such shootings every day. In the same year, the country recorded a record 39 mass shootings in which four or more people were killed.

The weapons are not incidental to the death tolls. Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022 and Lewiston in 2023 were each carried out with AR-style semiautomatic rifles and the high-capacity magazines that feed them, and those three attacks alone killed 56 people.

For ten years, the federal assault weapons ban took those weapons off the market. It was allowed to expire in 2004, and the evidence since is unambiguous about what that cost. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass-shooting data from 1981 to 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban period. Independent research on gun massacres, those killing six or more people, found 37% fewer incidents and 43% fewer deaths during the ban decade than in the decade before it. After the ban lapsed, the trend reversed.

A modern ban must learn from the 1994 law. It should cover the current generation of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that make them so lethal, rather than a list of models defined two decades before the newest rifles reached the market. Public support already exists: 64% of Americans favor banning assault weapons, and 66% favor banning high-capacity magazines.

## 5. Recommendations

Congress should act on four measures this session.

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales, online sales and sales at gun shows, with no exceptions for unlicensed sellers. The evidence from the states shows what is at stake: a 40% reduction in firearm homicide rates where checks cover every purchase, and a 25% increase where they were rolled back.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban on the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and pair it with a prohibition on large-capacity magazines, with definitions written to cover the weapons now on the market rather than those of the 1990s. During the last ban, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Restore sustained federal funding for firearm injury prevention research at no less than the $25 million Congress first appropriated in fiscal 2020, split evenly between the two agencies. That was the first federal research funding in more than 20 years, and it should never lapse again.

4. **Help states adopt and enforce extreme-risk laws.** Provide grants to states that enact and operate extreme-risk protection order laws, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be a danger to themselves or others. Indiana's law was followed by a 7.5% reduction in firearm suicides, and Connecticut's by a 13.7% reduction once enforcement increased.

The toll of 46,728 is not a fact of American life. It is the measurable cost of two gaps in federal law, and Congress alone has the power to close them.
"}

Good enough: "Since 1994" is fine and accurate for the Brady Act's effective date.

{"content": "# Data Appendix - Safer Communities Brief No. 9

Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban
Northgate Progress Institute | Publication date: Oct. 27, 2026
Prepared for editorial review: Oct. 2026

Data vintage note: All national mortality figures in this package use 2023, the reference year in the author's source tables (CDC final mortality data analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025). CDC final data for 2024 were released in February 2026 and show 44,447 total gun deaths, 27,593 gun suicides and 15,364 gun homicides. The editor should confirm with the author whether the brief is refreshed to 2024 before release.

Source line format per NPI style sheet: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.

---

## Table A1. National gun deaths, 2023 (head toll)

| Measure | 2023 |
|---|---|
| Total gun deaths, all intents | 46,728 |
| Firearm suicides | 27,300 (58%) |
| Firearm homicides | 17,927 (38%) |
| Legal intervention | 604 |
| Unintentional | 463 |
| Undetermined | 434 |
| Gun homicide trend | 20,958 (2021); 19,651 (2022); 17,927 (2023) |

Notes: 46,728 is the third-highest annual total on record, equivalent to one gun death every 11 minutes. Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995. Intent breakdown is presented here per style sheet B2 and is not repeated in body copy.

Sources:
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Underlying Cause of Death, WONDER Online Database (1999-2023), accessed Oct. 2026, https://wonder.cdc.gov/
- Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Gun Violence in the United States 2023: Examining the Gun Suicide Epidemic, June 26, 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf
- Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, New Report Highlights U.S. 2023 Gun Deaths: Suicide by Firearm at Record Levels for Third Straight Year, June 26, 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2025/new-report-highlights-us-2023-gun-deaths-suicide-by-firearm-at-record-levels-for-third-straight-year

Chart spec: Teal #0F6E6E for total deaths, coral #E4572E for the homicide trend line; y-axis starts at zero.

---

## Table A2. Children and teens

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Gun deaths, ages 1-17, 2023 | 2,566 |
| Rate per 100,000, ages 1-17, 2023 | 3.7 |
| Years as leading cause of death, ages 1-17 | 4th consecutive year |
| Gun deaths by intent, ages 1-17, 2023 | Homicide 63%; suicide 29%; unintentional 5%; undetermined/other 3% |
| Deaths by age band, 2023 | 1-4: 118; 5-9: 116; 10-14: 530; 15-17: 1,802 |
| Rate per 100,000, ages 1-19 (2021-2023 pooled) | 5.9 |

Notes: Per style sheet B3, body copy uses the phrase "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; the age range behind that claim is 1-17, and guns have led all causes of death for that group since 2020, accounting for more deaths than car crashes, overdoses or cancer. The "seven every day" line in the brief is 2,566 divided by 365. The 1-19 measure is a three-year pooled rate and covers a slightly wider age band; it is included for state and international comparisons, not as the headline figure. For some single-year age bands within 1-17, firearms are among the leading causes but not the top cause.

Sources:
- Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Annual Gun Violence Data 2023, June 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/data/annual-gun-violence-data-2023
- America's Health Rankings, United Health Foundation, Firearm Deaths - Children (ages 1-19, 2021-2023), 2024, https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/firearm_deaths_children
- KFF, Child and Teen Firearm Mortality in the U.S. and Peer Countries, July 18, 2023, https://www.kff.org/mental-health/child-and-teen-firearm-mortality-in-the-u-s-and-peer-countries/

---

## Table A3. Background checks (house estimate per style sheet B4)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Recent firearm acquisitions made without a background check | 22% (95% CI, 16%-27%) |
| Private-scope acquisitions made without a background check | 50% (95% CI, 35%-65%) |
| Same measure, states that regulate private sales | 26% (95% CI, 5%-47%) |
| Same measure, states that do not regulate private sales | 57% (95% CI, 40%-75%) |

Notes: The 22% figure is the house estimate per style sheet B4. It is the share of gun owners who acquired their most recent firearm within the previous two years who reported doing so without a background check, from a 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners. "Private-scope" means acquisitions other than from a store or pawnshop, including sales between individuals in person, online or at gun shows. The survey asks about owners' most recent acquisition and is subject to recall and reporting error; confidence intervals are wide on the private-sale subgroups. An earlier and much-cited 1994 estimate (Cook and Ludwig, ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer) is not used in this package: it counted gifts and inheritances and did not ask whether a background check occurred.

Sources:
- Miller, M., Hepburn, L. and Azrael, D., Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey, Jan. 4, 2017, https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M16-1590 (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017;166(4):233-239)
- Cook, P. and Ludwig, J., Guns in America: National Survey on Private Ownership and Use of Firearms, 1994, https://www.ncjrs.gov/pdffiles/165476.pdf

Chart spec: Teal #0F6E6E for the 22% headline bar, coral #E4572E for the 26% vs 57% state-law contrast; y-axis starts at zero.

---

## Table A4. Mass shootings, 2023

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Mass shootings (4+ victims shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter) | 656 |
| People killed in those incidents | 712 |
| People injured in those incidents | 2,692 |
| People killed or injured | 3,404 |
| Mass shootings with 4+ fatalities (record for the series) | 39 |

Notes: Gun Violence Archive definition: an incident in which four or more people are shot, killed or injured, excluding the shooter. The count includes incidents with no deaths, family-related incidents and gang-related incidents, and it is not comparable to databases that count only fatalities. The AP/USA Today/Northeastern mass-killing database uses a different definition (four or more killed, any weapon) and recorded 36 firearm incidents as of late October 2023; its year-end count was 39 mass shootings with four or more fatalities, the highest on record. The two counts answer different questions and should not be mixed in one sentence.

Sources:
- Gun Violence Archive, Mass Shootings in 2023, accessed Oct. 2026, https://www.gunviolencearchive.org/reports/mass-shooting?year=2023
- The Trace, Gun Violence by the Numbers in 2023, Dec. 31, 2023, https://www.thetrace.org/2023/12/data-gun-violence-deaths-america/
- Axios, Mass shootings increased in 2023. But gun deaths went down, Jan. 9, 2024, https://www.axios.com/2024/01/09/mass-shooting-gun-violence-us-2023
- Northeastern University, Record number of U.S. mass shootings in 2023, Jan. 3, 2024, https://news.northeastern.edu/2024/01/03/us-mass-shootings-in-2023/

---

## Table A5. The 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban and mass-casualty lethality

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Likelihood of mass-shooting fatalities during the ban period | 70% less likely (relative rate 0.30; 95% CI, 0.22-0.39) |
| Gun massacres (6+ killed) during the ban decade vs. the prior decade | 37% fewer incidents |
| Gun massacre deaths during the ban decade vs. the prior decade | 43% fewer deaths |
| Assault rifles' share of fatalities in the incidents where they were used | 430 of 501 fatalities (85.8%) across 44 incidents |

Notes: The ban, in force from September 1994 to September 2004, prohibited the manufacture and civilian sale of a defined set of semiautomatic firearms and large-capacity magazines and lapsed in 2004. The first row is from a peer-reviewed analysis of open-source mass-shooting data covering 1981 to 2017, which compares the ban period with non-ban periods while controlling for trend; it is an observational study of a single national policy change, not a randomized trial. Klarevas' figures compare the ban decade with the preceding decade for incidents killing six or more people.

Sources:
- DiMaggio, C. et al., Changes in US mass shooting deaths associated with the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban: Analysis of open-source data, Jan. 1, 2019, https://doi.org/10.1097/ta.0000000000002060 (Journal of Trauma and Acute Care Surgery, 2019;86(1):125-133)
- Klarevas, L., Rampage Nation: Ensuring American Citizens' Safety from Mass Shootings, 2016, https://www.tc.columbia.edu/articles/2021/march/tcs-louis-klarevas-supports-bidens-call-to-re-ban-assault-weapons-and-high-capacity-magazines/

---

## Table A6. Named incidents referenced in the brief

| Incident | Date | Killed | Weapon |
|---|---|---|---|
| Marjory Stoneman Douglas High School, Parkland, Florida | Feb. 14, 2018 | 17 | AR-style semiautomatic rifle |
| Robb Elementary School, Uvalde, Texas | May 24, 2022 | 21 (19 students and 2 teachers) | AR-style semiautomatic rifle |
| Lewiston, Maine | Oct. 25, 2023 | 18 (13 wounded) | AR-style semiautomatic rifles |

Notes: Fatality counts exclude the perpetrators. The three incidents killed 56 people in total. Weapon details are as documented by the Violence Policy Center and AP reporting.

Sources:
- Associated Press/USA Today/Northeastern University, Mass Killing Database, updated Aug. 20, 2024, https://cssh.northeastern.edu/crj/associated-press-usa-today-northeastern-university-mass-killing-database/
- Northeastern University, Record number of U.S. mass shootings in 2023, Jan. 3, 2024, https://news.northeastern.edu/2024/01/03/us-mass-shootings-in-2023/
- Violence Policy Center, Large Capacity Ammunition Magazines: Mass Shootings in the United States Involving High-Capacity Magazines, accessed Oct. 2026, https://www.vpc.org/fact_sht/VPCshootinglist.pdf

## Table A7. State policy evidence

| Policy change | Estimated effect |
|---|---|
| Connecticut permit-to-purchase law, 1995 | 40% reduction in firearm homicide rates over the first 10 years |
| Missouri repeal of handgun purchaser licensing, 2007 | 25% increase in firearm homicide rates |

| Connecticut risk-based firearm seizure law, after enforcement increased | 13.7% reduction in firearm suicides |

Notes: The Connecticut and Missouri homicide estimates use synthetic control methods, which compare each state with a weighted combination of states chosen to match pre-law trends; they estimate association rather than proven causation, and the Missouri estimate is from a separate study by a different team. The suicide estimates are from a quasi-experimental state panel analysis covering 1981 to 2015. Body copy rounds 13.7% to "a 13.7% reduction"; Bothell fact-checking should treat 13.7% as the precise figure, not 14%.

- Kivisto, A. J. and Phalen, P. L., Effects of Risk-Based Firearm Seizure Laws in Connecticut and Indiana on Suicide Rates, 1981-2015, August 2018, https://www.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.201700250 (Psychiatric Services, 2018;69(8):855-862)

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Publication date: Oct. 27, 2026

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes and the third-highest annual total ever recorded in the United States. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens, who lost 2,566 young lives in a single year.
- The two gaps that matter most are still open. Twenty-two percent of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and in 2023 the country recorded 656 mass shootings that killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more.
- Congress can close both gaps. Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban rest on decades of evidence and command overwhelming public support, including 92% of registered voters who back background checks for every gun buyer.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, the United States lost 46,728 people to gun violence, one death every 11 minutes and the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That figure is not a one-year aberration. It is the most recent data point in a crisis that has taken more than 45,000 American lives every year for the better part of a decade, and it leaves behind families, classrooms and workplaces that will never be whole.

Each of those deaths was preventable in the way that public health professionals use that word: there are known policies, tested in the states and in federal law, that measurably reduce gun deaths. The United States does not lack solutions. It lacks the two that cover the largest share of the problem. Federal law still leaves millions of gun sales outside the background check system, and the category of firearm built to fire the most rounds the fastest has been unregulated at the federal level since the assault weapons ban expired in 2004.

A full breakdown of gun deaths by intent, with the underlying CDC data and methodology notes, appears in the data appendix published with this brief.

## 2. Children and teens

The most sobering measure of this crisis is its age. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for American children and teens, killing more young people than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens died by gunfire, an average of seven every day.

The United States has by far the highest rate of child and teen firearm deaths among peer nations. In no other comparably large and wealthy country are firearms even among the top four causes of death for children and teens, let alone the first. The age range and intent breakdown for these figures appear in the data appendix.

Every day that Congress leaves the background check loophole and the assault weapons market intact, seven more families join a grief that policy could have prevented. That is the standard against which inaction should be measured.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a gun is sold by a federally licensed dealer. It has never required one for the sale that happens next door to the dealer's table: the private sale at a gun show, the listing on an online marketplace, the transfer between strangers in a parking lot. In most of the country, a person prohibited from buying a gun can buy one the same day, no questions asked.

The best national estimate of how often that happens comes from a 2015 survey of more than 1,600 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among guns acquired through private channels, the share without a background check was 50%. The gap is a matter of law, not behavior. In states that regulate private sales, 26% of such acquisitions occurred without a check. In states that do not, 57% did.

Closing the gap works. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which puts a background check in front of every handgun sale, was followed by a 40% reduction in the state's firearm homicide rate over its first decade. When Missouri repealed a comparable law in 2007, its firearm homicide rate rose 25%.

This is not a close political question. Ninety-two percent of registered voters, and clear majorities of gun owners, support requiring background checks for all gun buyers. The only constituency for the status quo is the loophole itself.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings have become a routine of American life, and the numbers no longer shock the way they should. In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in which four or more people were shot, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692. More than 3,400 people were shot in mass shootings in a single year, an average of nearly two such shootings every day. In the same year, the country recorded a record 39 mass shootings in which four or more people were killed.

The weapons are not incidental to the death tolls. Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022 and Lewiston in 2023 were each carried out with AR-style semiautomatic rifles and the high-capacity magazines that feed them, and those three attacks alone killed 56 people.

For ten years, the federal assault weapons ban took those weapons off the market. It was allowed to expire in 2004, and the evidence since is unambiguous about what that cost. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass-shooting data from 1981 to 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban period. Independent research on gun massacres, those killing six or more people, found 37% fewer incidents and 43% fewer deaths during the ban decade than in the decade before it. After the ban lapsed, the trend reversed.

A modern ban must learn from the 1994 law. It should cover the current generation of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that make them so lethal, rather than a list of models defined two decades before the newest rifles reached the market. Public support already exists: 64% of Americans favor banning assault weapons, and 66% favor banning high-capacity magazines.

## 5. Recommendations

Congress should act on four measures this session.

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales, online sales and sales at gun shows, with no exceptions for unlicensed sellers. The evidence from the states shows what is at stake: a 40% reduction in firearm homicide rates where checks cover every purchase, and a 25% increase where they were rolled back.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban on the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and pair it with a prohibition on large-capacity magazines, with definitions written to cover the weapons now on the market rather than those of the 1990s. During the last ban, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Restore sustained federal funding for firearm injury prevention research at no less than the $25 million Congress first appropriated in fiscal 2020, split evenly between the two agencies. That was the first federal research funding in more than 20 years, and it should never lapse again.

4. **Help states adopt and enforce extreme-risk laws.** Provide grants to states that enact and operate extreme-risk protection order laws, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be a danger to themselves or others. Indiana's law was followed by a 7.5% reduction in firearm suicides, and Connecticut's by a 13.7% reduction once enforcement increased.

The toll of 46,728 is not a fact of American life. It is the measurable cost of two gaps in federal law, and Congress alone has the power to close them.

# Data Appendix - Safer Communities Brief No. 9

Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban
Northgate Progress Institute | Publication date: Oct. 27, 2026
Prepared for editorial review: Oct. 2026

Data vintage note: All national mortality figures in this package use 2023, the reference year in the author's source tables (CDC final mortality data analyzed by the Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, June 2025). CDC final data for 2024 were released in February 2026 and show 44,447 total gun deaths, 27,593 gun suicides and 15,364 gun homicides. The editor should confirm with the author whether the brief is refreshed to 2024 before release.

Source line format per NPI style sheet: Agency/author, Title, Date, URL.

---

## Table A1. National gun deaths, 2023 (head toll)

| Measure | 2023 |
|---|---|
| Total gun deaths, all intents | 46,728 |
| Firearm suicides | 27,300 (58%) |
| Firearm homicides | 17,927 (38%) |
| Legal intervention | 604 |
| Unintentional | 463 |
| Undetermined | 434 |
| Gun homicide trend | 20,958 (2021); 19,651 (2022); 17,927 (2023) |
| Total gun deaths by year | 45,222 (2020); 48,830 (2021); 48,204 (2022); 46,728 (2023); 44,447 (2024) |

Notes: 46,728 is the third-highest annual total on record, equivalent to one gun death every 11 minutes. The brief's line that the crisis has killed more than 44,000 people every year since 2020 is drawn from the by-year row above; 2024 is the most recent year of final CDC data. Suicides have been the majority of gun deaths every year since 1995. Intent breakdown is presented here per style sheet B2 and is not repeated in body copy.

Sources:
- Centers for Disease Control and Prevention, Underlying Cause of Death, WONDER Online Database (1999-2023), accessed Oct. 2026, https://wonder.cdc.gov/
- Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Gun Violence in the United States 2023: Examining the Gun Suicide Epidemic, June 26, 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/sites/default/files/2025-06/2023-cgvs-gun-violence-in-the-united-states.pdf
- Johns Hopkins Bloomberg School of Public Health, New Report Highlights U.S. 2023 Gun Deaths: Suicide by Firearm at Record Levels for Third Straight Year, June 26, 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/2025/new-report-highlights-us-2023-gun-deaths-suicide-by-firearm-at-record-levels-for-third-straight-year
- Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Annual Gun Violence Data (2020-2024), accessed Oct. 2026, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/data/annual-gun-violence-data
- Pew Research Center, What the data says about gun deaths in the US, Apr. 28, 2026, https://www.pewresearch.org/short-reads/2026/04/28/what-the-data-says-about-gun-deaths-in-the-us/

Chart spec: Teal #0F6E6E for total deaths, coral #E4572E for the homicide trend line; y-axis starts at zero.

---

## Table A2. Children and teens

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Gun deaths, ages 1-17, 2023 | 2,566 |
| Rate per 100,000, ages 1-17, 2023 | 3.7 |
| Years as leading cause of death, ages 1-17 | 4th consecutive year |
| Gun deaths by intent, ages 1-17, 2023 | Homicide 63%; suicide 29%; unintentional 5%; undetermined/other 3% |
| Deaths by age band, 2023 | 1-4: 118; 5-9: 116; 10-14: 530; 15-17: 1,802 |
| Rate per 100,000, ages 1-19 (2021-2023 pooled) | 5.9 |

Notes: The peer-nation comparison in body copy comes from KFF: the United States has by far the highest rate of child and teen firearm mortality among peer nations, and in no other comparably large, wealthy country are firearms among the top four causes of death for children and teens. Per style sheet B3, body copy uses the phrase "guns are the leading cause of death for children and teens"; the age range behind that claim is 1-17, and guns have led all causes of death for that group since 2020, accounting for more deaths than car crashes, overdoses or cancer. The "seven every day" line in the brief is 2,566 divided by 365. The 1-19 measure is a three-year pooled rate and covers a slightly wider age band; it is included for state and international comparisons, not as the headline figure. For some single-year age bands within 1-17, firearms are among the leading causes but not the top cause.

Sources:
- Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, Annual Gun Violence Data 2023, June 2025, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/data/annual-gun-violence-data-2023
- America's Health Rankings, United Health Foundation, Firearm Deaths - Children (ages 1-19, 2021-2023), 2024, https://www.americashealthrankings.org/explore/measures/firearm_deaths_children
- KFF, Child and Teen Firearm Mortality in the U.S. and Peer Countries, July 18, 2023, https://www.kff.org/mental-health/child-and-teen-firearm-mortality-in-the-u-s-and-peer-countries/

---

## Table A3. Background checks (house estimate per style sheet B4)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Recent firearm acquisitions made without a background check | 22% (95% CI, 16%-27%) |
| Private-scope acquisitions made without a background check | 50% (95% CI, 35%-65%) |
| Same measure, states that regulate private sales | 26% (95% CI, 5%-47%) |
| Same measure, states that do not regulate private sales | 57% (95% CI, 40%-75%) |

Notes: The 22% figure is the house estimate per style sheet B4. It is the share of gun owners who acquired their most recent firearm within the previous two years who reported doing so without a background check, from a 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners. "Private-scope" means acquisitions other than from a store or pawnshop, including sales between individuals in person, online or at gun shows. The survey asks about owners' most recent acquisition and is subject to recall and reporting error; confidence intervals are wide on the private-sale subgroups. An earlier and much-cited 1994 estimate (Cook and Ludwig, ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer) is not used in this package: i
... [4248 chars truncated] ...
tyle semiautomatic rifles |

Notes: Fatality counts exclude the perpetrators. The three incidents killed 56 people in total. Weapon details are as documented by the Violence Policy Center and AP reporting.

Sources:
- Associated Press/USA Today/Northeastern University, Mass Killing Database, updated Aug. 20, 2024, https://cssh.northeastern.edu/crj/associated-press-usa-today-northeastern-university-mass-killing-database/
- Northeastern University, Record number of U.S. mass shootings in 2023, Jan. 3, 2024, https://news.northeastern.edu/2024/01/03/us-mass-shootings-in-2023/
- Violence Policy Center, Large Capacity Ammunition Magazines: Mass Shootings in the United States Involving High-Capacity Magazines, accessed Oct. 2026, https://www.vpc.org/fact_sht/VPCshootinglist.pdf

---

## Table A7. State policy evidence

| Policy change | Estimated effect |
|---|---|
| Connecticut permit-to-purchase law, 1995 | 40% reduction in firearm homicide rates over the first 10 years |
| Missouri repeal of handgun purchaser licensing, 2007 | 25% increase in firearm homicide rates |
| Indiana risk-based firearm seizure law | 7.5% reduction in firearm suicides in the 10 years after enactment |
| Connecticut risk-based firearm seizure law, after enforcement increased | 13.7% reduction in firearm suicides |

Notes: The Connecticut and Missouri homicide estimates use synthetic control methods, which compare each state with a weighted combination of states chosen to match pre-law trends; they estimate association rather than proven causation, and the Missouri estimate is from a separate study by a different team. The suicide estimates are from a quasi-experimental state panel analysis covering 1981 to 2015; Connecticut's 13.7% figure refers to the period after enforcement increased following Virginia Tech, and the immediate post-passage effect was estimated at 1.6%. Advocacy materials that round 13.7% to 14% should be checked against this table.

Sources:
- Crifasi, C. K., Vernick, J. S. and Webster, D. W., Association Between Connecticut's Permit-to-Purchase Handgun Law and Homicides, July 9, 2015, https://ajph.aphapublications.org/doi/full/10.2105/AJPH.2015.302703 (American Journal of Public Health, 2015;105(10):e49-e54)
- Webster, D., Crifasi, C. K. and Vernick, J. S., Effects of the Repeal of Missouri's Handgun Purchaser Licensing Law on Homicides, March 6, 2014, https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC3978146/ (Journal of Urban Health, 2014;91(2):293-302)
- Kivisto, A. J. and Phalen, P. L., Effects of Risk-Based Firearm Seizure Laws in Connecticut and Indiana on Suicide Rates, 1981-2015, August 2018, https://www.psychiatryonline.org/doi/full/10.1176/appi.ps.201700250 (Psychiatric Services, 2018;69(8):855-862)

---

## Table A8. Public support

| Policy | Support |
|---|---|
| Background checks for all gun buyers | 92% of registered voters (Nov. 2023) |
| Support among gun owners for background checks on all sales | Strong majorities; support holds among gun owners and non-owners |
| Ban on assault-style weapons | 64% of U.S. adults (June 2023) |
| Ban on high-capacity magazines holding more than 10 rounds | 66% of U.S. adults (June 2023) |

Notes: The Quinnipiac question asks whether voters support "requiring background checks for all gun buyers." Pew's question asks about "banning assault-style weapons"; body copy uses the house term "assault weapons" for the policy and the appendix preserves the poll's wording. The gun-owner line reflects the Johns Hopkins 2023 national survey, which found support for background checks on all sales among both prior and new gun owners; the survey did not publish a single headline percentage for that item, so copy says "clear majorities" rather than a number.

Sources:
- Quinnipiac University Poll, National Trends (Registered Voters), Nov. 2, 2023, https://poll.qu.edu/images/polling/us/us11022023_regvoter_uecc53.pdf
- Pew Research Center, Americans' Views of Specific Gun Policy Proposals, June 28, 2023, https://www.pewresearch.org/politics/2023/06/28/americans-views-of-specific-gun-policy-proposals/
- Johns Hopkins Center for Gun Violence Solutions, National Survey of Gun Policy 2023, 2023, https://publichealth.jhu.edu/center-for-gun-violence-solutions/americans-agree-on-effective-gun-policy-more-than-were-led-to-believe

---

## Table A9. Federal gun violence research funding

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| First federal appropriation for gun violence research in more than 20 years | $25 million (fiscal 2020) |
| Split between agencies | $12.5 million CDC; $12.5 million NIH |

Notes: The appropriation was included in the fiscal 2020 Further Consolidated Appropriations Act (H.R. 1865) and was the first dedicated federal gun violence research funding since the mid-1990s.

Sources:
- U.S. Congress, Further Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2020 (H.R. 1865), signed Dec. 20, 2019, https://www.congress.gov/bill/116th-congress/house-bill/1865
- ABC News, Congress agrees on historic deal to fund $25 million in gun violence research, Dec. 16, 2019, https://abcnews.com/Health/congress-approves-unprecedented-25-million-gun-violence-research/story?id=67762555

---

## Table A10. Supplementary: rifles and homicide (not used in body copy)

| Year | Rifles as a share of murders | Murders committed with rifles |
|---|---|---|
| 2017 | 2.6% | not reported in source table |
| 2018 | 2.8% | 297 |

Notes: FBI Expanded Homicide Data do not separate AR-style rifles from all rifles, and not all agencies report weapon data. Held here for Q&A and for the editor's option under style sheet B6, which allows one sentence in body copy followed by a pivot to mass-casualty lethality. It is deliberately not used in the brief as drafted; the editor may wish to add the one-sentence treatment so that advocates are not caught unprepared by the figure.

Sources:

# Closing the gaps: The case for universal background checks and an assault weapons ban

Safer Communities Brief No. 9 | Northgate Progress Institute | Publication date: Oct. 27, 2026

By Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention

## Executive summary

- Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one person every 11 minutes and the third-highest annual total ever recorded in the United States. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens, who lost 2,566 young lives in a single year.
- The two gaps that matter most are still open. In the best available national estimate, from a 2015 survey, 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check, and in 2023 the country recorded 656 mass shootings that killed 712 people and injured 2,692 more.
- Congress can close both gaps. Universal background checks and an updated assault weapons ban rest on decades of evidence and command overwhelming public support, including 92% of registered voters who back background checks for every gun buyer.

## 1. The toll

In 2023, the United States lost 46,728 people to gun violence, one death every 11 minutes and the third-highest annual total ever recorded. That figure is not a one-year aberration. It is one year in a crisis that has killed more than 44,000 Americans annually since 2020, and it leaves behind families, classrooms and workplaces that will never be whole.

Each of those deaths was preventable in the way that public health professionals use that word: there are known policies, tested in the states and in federal law, that measurably reduce gun deaths. The United States does not lack solutions. It lacks the two that cover the largest share of the problem. Federal law still leaves private sales outside the background check system in most states, and the category of firearm built to fire the most rounds the fastest has been unregulated at the federal level since the assault weapons ban expired in 2004.

A full breakdown of gun deaths by intent, with the underlying CDC data and methodology notes, appears in the data appendix published with this brief.

## 2. Children and teens

The most sobering measure of this crisis is its age. For the fourth consecutive year, guns were the leading cause of death for American children and teens, killing more young people than car crashes, drug overdoses or cancer. In 2023, 2,566 children and teens died by gunfire, an average of seven every day.

The United States has by far the highest rate of child and teen firearm deaths among peer nations. In no other comparably large and wealthy country are firearms even among the top four causes of death for children and teens, let alone the first. The age range and intent breakdown for these figures appear in the data appendix.

Every day that Congress leaves the background check loophole and the assault weapons market intact, seven more families join a grief that policy could have prevented. That is the standard against which inaction should be measured.

## 3. The background-check gap

Since 1994, federal law has required a background check before a gun is sold by a federally licensed dealer. It has never required one for the sale that happens next door to the dealer's table: the private sale at a gun show, the listing on an online marketplace, the transfer between strangers in a parking lot. In most of the country, a person prohibited from buying a gun can buy one the same day, no questions asked.

The best national estimate of how often that happens comes from a 2015 survey of more than 1,600 gun owners published in the Annals of Internal Medicine: 22% of gun owners who acquired a firearm in the previous two years did so without a background check. Among guns acquired through private channels, the share without a background check was 50%. The gap is a matter of law, not behavior. In states that regulate private sales, 26% of such acquisitions occurred without a check. In states that do not, 57% did.

Closing the gap works. Connecticut's 1995 permit-to-purchase law, which puts a background check in front of every handgun sale, was followed by a 40% reduction in the state's firearm homicide rate over its first decade. When Missouri repealed a comparable law in 2007, its firearm homicide rate rose 25%.

This is not a close political question. In polling conducted in November 2023, 92% of registered voters, along with clear majorities of gun owners, supported requiring background checks for all gun buyers. The only constituency for the status quo is the loophole itself.

## 4. Mass shootings and assault weapons

Mass shootings have become a routine of American life, and the numbers no longer shock the way they should. In 2023, the Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in which four or more people were shot, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692. More than 3,400 people were shot in mass shootings in a single year, an average of nearly two such shootings every day. In the same year, the country recorded a record 39 mass shootings in which four or more people were killed.

The weapons are not incidental to the death tolls. Parkland in 2018, Uvalde in 2022 and Lewiston in 2023 were each carried out with AR-style semiautomatic rifles and the high-capacity magazines that feed them, and those three attacks alone killed 56 people.

For ten years, the federal assault weapons ban kept new assault weapons and large-capacity magazines out of the civilian market. It was allowed to expire in 2004, and the evidence since is unambiguous about what that cost. A peer-reviewed analysis of mass-shooting data from 1981 to 2017 found that mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely to occur during the ban period. Independent research on gun massacres, those killing six or more people, found 37% fewer incidents and 43% fewer deaths during the ban decade than in the decade before it. After the ban lapsed, the trend reversed.

A modern ban must learn from the 1994 law. It should cover the current generation of assault weapons and the large-capacity magazines that make them so lethal, rather than a list of models defined two decades before the newest rifles reached the market. Public support already exists: in 2023 polling, 64% of Americans favored banning assault weapons and 66% favored banning high-capacity magazines.

## 5. Recommendations

Congress should act on four measures this session.

1. **Pass universal background checks.** Require a background check on every firearm sale and transfer, including private sales, online sales and sales at gun shows, with no exceptions for unlicensed sellers. The evidence from the states shows what is at stake: a 40% reduction in firearm homicide rates where checks cover every purchase, and a 25% increase where they were rolled back.

2. **Reinstate and update the assault weapons ban.** Restore the federal ban on the manufacture and sale of assault weapons and pair it with a prohibition on large-capacity magazines, with definitions written to cover the weapons now on the market rather than those of the 1990s. During the last ban, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely.

3. **Fund gun violence research at the CDC and NIH.** Restore sustained federal funding for firearm injury prevention research at no less than the $25 million Congress first appropriated in fiscal 2020, split evenly between the two agencies. That was the first federal research funding in more than 20 years, and it should never lapse again.

4. **Help states adopt and enforce extreme-risk laws.** Provide grants to states that enact and operate extreme-risk protection order laws, which allow courts to temporarily remove firearms from people shown to be a danger to themselves or others. Indiana's law was followed by a 7.5% reduction in firearm suicides, and Connecticut's by a 13.7% reduction once enforcement increased.

The toll of 46,728 is not a fact of American life. It is the measurable cost of two gaps in federal law, and Congress alone has the power to close them.

The "seven every day" line in the brief is 2,566 divided by 365. The 1-19 measure is a three-year pooled rate and covers a slightly wider age band; it is included for state and international comparisons, not as the headline figure. For some single-year age bands within 1-17, firearms are among the leading causes but not the top cause.

## Table A3. Background checks (house estimate per style sheet B4)

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Recent firearm acquisitions made without a background check | 22% (95% CI, 16%-27%) |
| Private-scope acquisitions made without a background check | 50% (95% CI, 35%-65%) |
| Same measure, states that regulate private sales | 26% (95% CI, 5%-47%) |
| Same measure, states that do not regulate private sales | 57% (95% CI, 40%-75%) |

Notes: The 22% figure is the house estimate per style sheet B4. It is the share of gun owners who acquired their most recent firearm within the previous two years who reported doing so without a background check, from a 2015 national survey of 1,613 gun owners. "Private-scope" means acquisitions other than from a store or pawnshop, including sales between individuals in person, online or at gun shows. The survey asks about owners' most recent acquisition and is subject to recall and reporting error; confidence intervals are wide on the private-sale subgroups. An earlier and much-cited 1994 estimate (Cook and Ludwig, ~40% of recently acquired guns obtained without going through a licensed dealer) is not used in this package: it counted gifts and inheritances and did not ask whether a background check occurred.

Sources:
- Miller, M., Hepburn, L. and Azrael, D., Firearm Acquisition Without Background Checks: Results of a National Survey, Jan. 4, 2017, https://www.acpjournals.org/doi/10.7326/M16-1590 (Annals of Internal Medicine, 2017;166(4):233-239)

## Table A5. The 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban and mass-casualty lethality

| Measure | Value |
|---|---|
| Likelihood of mass-shooting fatalities during the ban period | 70% less likely (relative rate 0.30; 95% CI, 0.22-0.39) |

Notes: The ban, in force from September 1994 to September 2004, prohibited the manufacture and civilian sale of a defined set of semiautomatic firearms and large-capacity magazines and lapsed in 2004. The first row is from a peer-reviewed analysis of open-source mass-shooting data covering 1981 to 2017, which compares the ban period with non-ban periods while controlling for trend; it is an observational study of a single national policy change, not a randomized trial. # Two gaps in federal law cost 46,728 American lives, new NPI brief finds

WASHINGTON, Oct. 27, 2026. The Northgate Progress Institute today released Safer Communities Brief No. 9, "Closing the Gaps: The Case for Universal Background Checks and an Assault Weapons Ban," by Dr. Jamal Whitfield, Senior Fellow for Gun Violence Prevention.

Gun violence killed 46,728 Americans in 2023, one every 11 minutes, and guns were the leading cause of death for the nation's children and teens for the fourth consecutive year. The Gun Violence Archive counted 656 mass shootings in 2023, killing 712 people and injuring 2,692 more.

"The two gaps in federal law have a body count," Dr. Whitfield said. "Twenty-two percent of gun owners who bought a gun in the previous two years faced no background check, and the ban that kept the deadliest rifles off the market expired in 2004. Congress has the evidence and 92% of voters behind it. What is missing is the will."

The brief calls on Congress to require background checks on every gun sale; to reinstate and update the assault weapons ban, including large-capacity magazines; to fund CDC and NIH gun violence research at no less than the $25 million first appropriated in fiscal 2020; and to help states adopt extreme-risk laws.

The evidence is already on the record. During the 1994-2004 federal assault weapons ban, mass-shooting fatalities were 70% less likely. Connecticut's permit-to-purchase law was followed by a 40% reduction in firearm homicide rates; Missouri's repeal of a comparable law was followed by a 25% increase.

"The United States does not lack solutions to gun violence," Dr. Whitfield said. "It lacks two of them, and both are sitting in a drawer on Capitol Hill."

The brief and its data appendix, with full definitions and source lines, are available at [NPI website].

The Northgate Progress Institute is a progressive policy think tank based in Washington, D.C. The Safer Communities series examines the evidence behind policies that reduce gun deaths and injuries.
